summary: Selection sort grows a sorted prefix by repeatedly selecting the smallest remaining element and swapping it into place. It does at most n-1 swaps, which is its one real advantage.

sections.heading: Algorithm
bullets: For position i from 0 to n-2, scan a[i..n-1] for the index of the minimum.
The prefix a[0..i] is now final; continue with the next position.

sections.heading: Walkthrough
sections.body: On [64, 25, 12, 22, 11]: the minimum 11 swaps with 64 giving [11, 25, 12, 22, 64]; next 12 swaps with 25 giving [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]; then 22, then done.

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Comparisons: always n(n-1)/2, so O(n²) in best, average, and worst cases.
Swaps: at most n-1, i.e. O(n).
Not adaptive: sorted input is not faster.

sections.heading: Stability
sections.body: The standard version is not stable. Swapping a distant minimum into position can jump over an equal element: [4a, 4b, 1] becomes [1, 4b, 4a]. A stable variant shifts elements instead of swapping, at the cost of more writes.
If writing is far costlier than reading (EEPROM, flash with limited erase cycles, large records), selection sort's O(n) swaps beat bubble and insertion sort's O(n²) writes, despite O(n²) comparisons.

subtopics.title: Relation to heap sort
subtopics.summary: Selection with a better data structure.

sections.body: Heap sort is selection sort where 'find the minimum' uses a heap in O(log n) instead of a linear scan, improving total time from O(n²) to O(n log n).

subtopics.title: Double selection
subtopics.summary: Find min and max each pass.

sections.body: Track both the minimum and the maximum in one scan and place them at both ends. Halves the number of passes, same O(n²) overall.
Cycle sort writes each element at most once to its final position, achieving the theoretical minimum number of writes, still O(n²) time.

takeaways: Select the minimum, swap it to the front, repeat.
Always O(n²) comparisons but only O(n) swaps.
In place, not stable, not adaptive.
Use when writes are expensive; otherwise prefer insertion or O(n log n) sorts.
